scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that laws need flexibility while arguing too much undermines fairness; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: A law that fits one situation perfectly may be cruel or absurd in another.
Some people argue that laws should be flexible enough to take account of different circumstances, times, and places.
I largely agree that laws need flexibility, but I believe too much flexibility can also undermine fairness.

sections.role: Body 1 — Why flexibility makes laws just

sentences.text: First, laws really do need some flexibility to be just.
No single rule can fairly cover every situation that life produces.
For example, a law against theft should treat a starving person differently from a greedy one.
This shows that flexible laws can deliver justice that rigid rules would miss.
Circumstances, times, and places change, and laws must adapt to remain fair.
A wise judge can use flexibility to fit the law to the real facts of a case.
To this extent, flexibility makes laws more just.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why too much flexibility harms

sentences.text: Second, however, too much flexibility can make laws unfair and unpredictable.
If laws bend too easily, people can never be sure what is truly allowed.
Consider a system where the same act is punished harshly for one person and ignored for another.
Such inconsistency shows that excessive flexibility can destroy equal treatment under the law.
Flexible laws can also be twisted by the powerful to escape the rules that bind others.
People need clear and steady laws they can understand and rely upon.
Flexibility, then, must be balanced by firm and consistent principles.
In conclusion, laws should be flexible enough to fit different circumstances fairly.
But too much flexibility undermines the consistency that justice requires.
The best laws balance sensible flexibility with clear and equal rules for all.
